raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 12-month old boy was referred from a clinic to the Kintampo Municipal Hospital (Kintampo, Ghana). He had presented at the clinic with a 2-day history of fever and vomiting. On admission to the clinic, diagnosis of severe anaemia secondary to Malaria was made. Despite treatment with IV fluid, IM Quinine and a blood transfusion, his condition deteriorated and he began to pass bloody stools. After two days he was referred to hospital for further management.
On arrival, the child had a reduced conscious level. He was febrile (39.5 C) and pale with pulse and respiration rates 110 beat/min and 60 breaths/min respectively. Abdominal examination was normal apart from periumbilical tenderness.
Blood film was positive for malaria parasites. Haemoglobin was 4.2g/dL and white blood cell count 16.4 x 109. Neither Widal test nor stool cultures were done. Supine abdominal X-ray showed air fluid levels. Erect chest X-ray showed no subphrenic gas. Treatment of severe anaemia secondary to malaria and suspected typhoid was continued. Intranasal oxygen, IV fluids and whole blood were administered along with paracetamol, IM quinine, IV gentamicin and IV metronidazole. After a further 2 days he remained semiconscious and febrile, passing blood clots in his stool. Despite transfusion, haemoglobin remained 4.3g/dL. Abdominal examination remained unremarkable.
An exploratory laparotomy was performed. On entering the peritoneum a large amount of blood-stained fluid was seen. A 1.5cm anterior perforation of the duodenal wall was found, with bleeding from the posterior duodenal wall (Figure 1). The bleeding vessel was clamped and the perforation closed using an omental patch.
Postoperatively the child received a further blood transfusion, antibiotics and IV ranitidine. Ten days post-operatively he was discharged. On follow-up he had no sequelae.
Due to resource constraint no test for Helicobacter pylori was performed. The mother denied giving any medication to the child.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 12-month-old male infant presenting with a 2-day history of fever, vomiting, severe anemia, and bloody stools.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The infant presented to a local clinic with a 2-day history of fever and vomiting. Despite treatment with intravenous fluids, intramuscular quinine, and a blood transfusion, his condition deteriorated and he began to pass bloody stools with altered consciousness, prompting hospital transfer after 2 days. On arrival at the municipal hospital, he was febrile, pale, and passed blood clots in his stool, with persistent severe anemia refractory to transfusion.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy. Received intravenous fluids, intramuscular quinine, and a blood transfusion at a local clinic prior to transfer. Mother denied administering any home medications.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, vomiting, bloody stools (passing blood clots), and reduced consciousness. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature: 39.5 C, pulse: 110 beats/min, respiratory rate: 60 breaths/min. Reduced conscious level, semiconscious; marked pallor. Abdomen: Periumbilical tenderness; otherwise unremarkable without overt peritoneal signs.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin: 4.2 g/dL (remained 4.3 g/dL after initial transfusion). White blood cell count: 16.4 x 10^9/L. Supine abdominal X-ray: Air-fluid levels. Erect chest X-ray: No subphrenic free gas. Widal test and stool cultures: Not performed.
objective.advanced_workup: Emergency exploratory laparotomy: Entering peritoneum revealed a large amount of blood-stained fluid; 1.5 cm anterior perforation of the duodenal wall with active bleeding from the posterior duodenal wall. (Helicobacter pylori testing not performed due to resource constraints).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Severe malaria complicated by profound anemia, duodenal ulcer perforation, active duodenal hemorrhage, and hemoperitoneum.
Diagnostic confirmation: Peripheral blood film was positive for malaria parasites. (Suspected typhoid fever was not confirmed microbiologically; Widal and stool cultures were not done).
Plan & Outcome: Emergency exploratory laparotomy with vascular clamping of the bleeding posterior duodenal wall and omental patch closure of the 1.5 cm anterior duodenal perforation. Medical management included intranasal oxygen, intravenous fluids, whole blood transfusions (pre- and postoperative), intramuscular quinine, intravenous gentamicin, intravenous metronidazole, intravenous ranitidine, and paracetamol. The child recovered uneventfully and was discharged 10 days postoperatively without sequelae.
